Structural fixed features explicitly required by the contract are allowed."},"candidate_prose":"The sea dragon crouched beneath the lighthouse windows, seawater shining on her blue-green scales. Daylight flashed on the brass compass held carefully between her teeth.

Ekin took one step forward. “That’s mine.”

The dragon turned away. With a slow dip of her head, she placed the compass in a nest of dry rope and sailcloth beside the wall. Ekin saw its scratched lid gleam between the folds, close enough to make her fingers ache.

“There,” she whispered. “I can reach it.”

Duru caught her sleeve. “Wait.”

Ekin pulled free. “Stop telling me to wait.”

Duru was not looking at the compass. She pointed beyond the nest. Something small stirred under a loop of rope.

A cat-sized dragon hatchling crawled into the daylight. Its wings opened and flapped, but they could not lift it. It stumbled over the cloth, then settled beside the compass, plainly unhurt.

Ekin stared. “Oh.”

The mother dragon moved at once. She planted herself across the approach to the nest, wings half spread from wall to wall. Her tail struck the floor with a heavy thump. Ekin stopped, watching the long body seal off every direct path to the compass.

“I warned you,” Duru said quietly.

“And it’s right there,” Ekin snapped. “Grandfather’s compass is right there.”

A gust moaned through the open lighthouse door below. Both girls glanced toward the narrow turning stair that curled down from the upper room. Through its rails they could see the lower maintenance room and, in the sea-facing wall, a fixed iron grate washed with gray light.

Duru studied the stair, then the dragon. “Rushing her won’t work.”

Ekin clenched her hands inside her jacket pockets. The compass shone beside the hatchling while the mother dragon watched them.

“Then think faster,” Ekin said.","deterministic_findings":[]}
